extracted.intended_audience: medical students and faculty at a Catholic university; Catholic educators and clergy
extracted.subtask_description: A university address arguing how the medical profession should relate to moral and religious authority, especially within a Catholic university context; it gives normative principles for professional scope, conflicts between sciences, and the Church’s role in education. Targeted at physicians, medical students, and university faculty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchy of sciences / subordination principle
rubrics_metrics.description: When different professions or 'sciences' (e.g., military art, statesmanship, medicine, religion) conflict, the science concerned with the higher ends (politics, morals, religion) must prevail; the lower science must yield.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by soldier vs. statesman (commander yielding to governor-general) and medical man vs. priest (physician enunciating medical certainty but yielding to higher moral/religious duty). The text emphasizes that success in a lower art does not trump the claims of a superior science when ends conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define the proper province of Medicine
rubrics_metrics.description: Medicine's proper province is the physical nature of man: the preservation and restoration of bodily health; it limits itself by profession to the health of the body and to ascertaining causes and means of cure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This delimitation is used to show both the legitimate authority of medical truth within its domain and its limits relative to moral and religious considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Health must give way to duty
rubrics_metrics.description: Bodily health is not the highest end of man; when duty (moral/religious obligations) conflicts with preservation of health, duty takes precedence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete example: a Sister of Charity who remains in a fever-stricken place at the command of ecclesiastical superiors — the medical adviser was right medically, but the Sister was not wrong morally. The point: medical rightness does not compel obedience where higher duties obtain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject the sophism 'what is true is lawful' across sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: The fallacy is to assume that what is true in one science (e.g., medicine) is thereby lawful or obligatory in another (e.g., religion or morals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author warns medical practitioners against assuming medical truth entails moral permissibility — what is true in medicine may be unlawful or inappropriate in consequence of higher moral/religious laws. The passage stresses careful recognition of competing truths rather than unqualified application of one discipline’s maxims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize differing evidentiary weight of moral/religious truths
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral and religious facts are less obtrusive and have a more delicate, variable presence in consciousness than physical facts; conscience and faith are fickle and require protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because conscience and faith are 'faint shadows' compared with the luminous evidence of physical science, they can be easily suppressed by continuous impression from material facts. Therefore institutions or safeguards (e.g., the Church) are needed to preserve these higher truths in professionals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional formation must preserve awareness of higher sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: Medical education should guard against the profession so engrossing the mind that practitioners forget or become 'dead' to moral and religious truths; physicians must not view man solely as an animal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning that a narrowly trained medical philosopher may give advice 'insufferable to any religious mind' because he neglects the soul; the remedy is cultivation of awareness of other branches of knowledge (morals/religion) during professional formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Catholic Church as the institutional defender of moral and religious truths
rubrics_metrics.description: The Church provides a visible, continuous, local guardian for conscience and faith — the only reliable champion against the overpowering immediacy of physical facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Church is presented as necessary because moral and religious intimations are fragile; historical longevity (eighteen hundred years) and its persistent activity in defending these truths are offered as grounds for its authority and role in education and society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bring the Faculty of Medicine under the Church's safeguard (context-specific recommendation)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is highly desirable — especially in a country like Ireland — that the Faculty of Medicine be brought under the 'shadow' or protection of the Catholic Church so that scientific growth is accompanied by religious fidelity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an explicit institutional prescription: in countries with strong Catholic tradition, medical science should not 'run wild' but should grow in religion; the Church’s oversight helps prevent the profession from losing sight of higher duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust and loyalty to ecclesiastical authority in professional judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Physicians and medical faculty should trust the Church implicitly, even when their private judgment might differ, remembering the Church’s long experience and claim to transmit moral truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author urges gratitude and loyal devotion to the Church, and counsel to accept its prudence and correctness as tested by centuries, making such trust part of professional conduct within a Catholic university setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of medical faculty as mediators between Religion and Science
rubrics_metrics.description: The medical faculty’s high office is to act as links between Religion and Science — to help transmit religious truths alongside scientific knowledge to future generations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appeal to medical educators to take up this responsibility with joy and to assist the Church in preserving and transmitting faith while pursuing scientific knowledge.
